title: Hubble Interacting Galaxy Arp 256
caption: Merging galaxy pair Arp 256, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Arp 256, VV 352, MCG-02-01-051 · constellation Cetus · about 350 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration, and A. Evans (University of Virginia, Charlottesville/NRAO/Stony Brook University)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Two spiral galaxies with badly disrupted shapes are scattered with blue knots of star formation, so many that NASA compares them to exploding fireworks. The galaxy on the left trails two long, ribbon-like tails of gas, dust and stars. This is Arp 256, a pair in the early stages of merging.

NASA calls the blue knots sites of star formation, and young, hot stars give off blue light. Ribbon-like tails such as those on the left are typically tidal features, drawn out of a galaxy's outer regions by a partner's gravity.

Arp 256 is a luminous infrared system, pouring out over a hundred billion times as much energy as our Sun. It lies about 350 million light-years away in Cetus, the Whale, and Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies lists it as entry 256.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys used a blue filter, F435W (B), and a near-infrared filter, F814W (I). NASA shows F435W in blue, F814W in red, and a blend of the two in green.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter captures light outside human vision, and the system's strong infrared glow is invisible to the eye.

explore: The image is part of a set of 59 merging-galaxy pictures released for its 18th anniversary in April 2008. The system is also cataloged as VV 352. NASA describes such collisions as playing out over several hundred million years.
alt: Two distorted spiral galaxies dotted with many blue knots, the left one trailing two long ribbon-like tails.
